Under s 40 of the Probate and Administration Act 1898 (NSW), where one of multiple executors predeceases the testator, the surviving executor(s) may apply for probate and administer the estate alone. If all named executors predecease the testator or renounce, the Court may grant letters of administration with the will annexed under s 74 to the person entitled to the residuary estate, or another appropriate person.

messages.content: Can a beneficiary who killed the testator inherit under the will in NSW?

No. Under s 65 of the Succession Act 2006 (NSW) (the forfeiture rule), a person who has unlawfully killed another person is not entitled to acquire any benefit as a result of the killing, including under the deceased's will or on intestacy. Under s 66, the Court may modify the effect of the forfeiture rule if satisfied that justice requires it, having regard to the conduct of the offender and the deceased, the effect of the rule on other persons, and any other relevant matter. This discretion does not apply to murder.

messages.content: What is the difference between a specific legacy, a general legacy, and a demonstrative legacy in Australian succession law?

A specific legacy is a gift of a particular identified item ('my Rolex watch') — it is subject to ademption if the item no longer exists at death. A general legacy is a gift of a quantity not identified with particular assets ('$50,000') — it is paid from the general estate and abates proportionally if the estate is insufficient. A demonstrative legacy is a general amount directed to be paid from a specific fund ('$50,000 from my ANZ account') — if the fund is insufficient, the balance is paid from the general estate. These distinctions affect priority in abatement under s 46 of the Probate and Administration Act 1898 (NSW).
